A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NNsight and NDIF, with matching central architecture and examples. Text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. v2 includes readable Appendices A–E; v1 ends with references and has no appendix.

before.justification: v1 Section 6 and Table 1 report original activation-patching and attribution-patching runtime experiments across models and libraries.

after.justification: v2 reports original library and remote-service benchmarks, concurrent-user testing, and an analysis of 184 research papers in Section 2 and Appendix A.

M1.justification: The core tracing, intervention graphs, Envoy/Proxy access and sessions remain. The reported serving procedure changes: v1 Section 3 says multiple users can be batched, whereas v2 Appendices B.2/D.2 specify queued execution with one forward pass per user and defer shared batching to future work. The PDFs do not establish whether implementation changed or the earlier description was corrected.

E1.justification: v2 adds a research-usage analysis covering 184 papers and evaluates standard remote inference, remote interventions and concurrent-user workloads. Attribution-patching timing evaluation disappears, although example code remains. IOI is newly identified as benchmark data; v1's unnamed 32-example batch does not establish whether the underlying dataset changed.

E2.justification: Petals becomes an evaluated comparator in Figure 6c, having appeared only in related work in v1. v2 also introduces direct HPC-versus-NDIF comparisons. The local baukit, pyvene and TransformerLens comparison remains, with TransformerLens now participating in the Gemma comparison where v1 reported missing results.

E3.justification: Table 1 changes from eight A100 GPUs with CUDA 12.4 to four H100 GPUs with CUDA 12.3, and replaces Llama3-70B with Llama-3.1-8B; both versions specify 32-example batches. New protocols measure setup time, sweep OPT model sizes, compare private Petals/NDIF deployments, and test concurrent requests over 30-second windows. The survey adds paper-selection and MMLU-imputation procedures.

E4.justification: v2 adds workload stress testing with 1–100 concurrent users in Appendix D.2, examining response-time growth and variability. Figure 6 analyzes setup and communication costs across OPT sizes. Appendix A additionally compares research-model and released-model size distributions. These analyses extend substantially beyond v1's library runtime comparison.

E5.justification: v1 already reports values with ± notation but provides no sample count or interval definition. v2 Figure 6 specifies n=128 and discusses 95% confidence intervals; Figure 10 reports medians, quartiles and extrema. These improve statistical documentation without establishing increased repetitions of the earlier experiments.

E6.justification: Table 1 contains replacement timings under changed hardware/model settings: for example, NNsight's Gemma activation-patching time changes from 0.337 to 0.227 seconds. Attribution timings disappear, while setup, remote-service, survey and load-testing results are added. v2 Table 2 reports OPT-66B HPC/NDIF setup times of 23.697/0.423 seconds but request times of 1.889/2.739 seconds, distinguishing setup savings from request latency.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.1 adds formal computation/intervention-graph definitions, getter/setter edges and an acyclicity condition. Appendix E supplies a constructive equivalence argument between multiple-output and single-output apply nodes. v1 describes graph implementation without these mathematical definitions or derivations.

C1.justification: v2 adds a headline claim that its quantitative survey reveals a growing capability gap in interpretability research. It also presents the intervention-graph architecture as an explicit contribution centered on separating experiments from deployment and improving reproducibility, alongside NNsight and NDIF. v1 primarily presents the library and service; their original access and flexibility claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of the research gap and remote-service costs, and explicitly limits current co-tenancy to sequential execution in its appendices. v1's graph-optimization and high-level-abstraction limitation discussions disappear, while the closed-model restriction remains. Section 4 also introduces a runtime-benefit claim for larger models that is not supported by Table 2's request latencies.

D1.justification: Appendices B–D substantially expand documentation of Ray routing, model sharding, distributed tensor handling, memory management, protocols and benchmark implementation. Additional examples cover LoRA training, gradient manipulation and remote probing; Appendix A documents survey curation. Conversely, v1's NNsight 0.2 syntax note and specific NDIF early-access eligibility/application instructions are omitted.

R1.justification: The main positioning against Garçon, Petals and local intervention libraries remains. v2 extends it with S-LoRA, dLoRA and Punica, distinguishing their adapter-serving scope from general interventions, and adds sources supporting the survey and distributed implementation. Some background citations disappear. Publication updates to existing works such as Petals do not constitute new related work.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and the tutorial-oriented main text is reorganized around a survey, formal framework, evaluation and discussion. Much implementation material moves into Appendix B, with expanded examples in Appendix C. Separate ecosystem and limitations sections disappear, and ethics and reproducibility statements are added.

P2.justification: v2 adds survey plots, formal graph and infrastructure diagrams, a side-by-side code comparison, benchmark plots, a load-testing plot and three appendix tables. Table 1 replaces its attribution-patching block with setup times. The remote-pipeline diagram is substantially expanded, while v1's Envoy diagram is retained as v2 Figure 9.

improvement.justification: v1's central remote-service benefits were largely asserted while its benchmark evaluated local libraries. v2 directly tests setup costs, remote interventions, Petals comparisons and concurrent demand, substantially strengthening evidence for the system's practical value. Formal definitions and expanded implementation documentation also improve assessability. Removing attribution-patching benchmarks and some limitations weakens coverage, and the runtime-benefit wording overstates Table 2, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial gain in validation of the paper's central contribution.
